findings.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java:44 — P1 confidence 100: adding the abstract SPI method `int order();` breaks every previously compiled external `CryptoProvider`, because `Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order)` invokes the absent implementation during initialization and terminates provider discovery with `AbstractMethodError`.

common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:30 — P1 confidence 75: the global first-writer guard `if (cryptoProvider == null)` permanently installs `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` when `AuthzClient` initializes through a loader that sees only its service, so later common-crypto calls deterministically reach one of its 17 `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.");` branches even after a full provider becomes visible.

common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — P1 confidence 75: `.sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())` assigns the Default, Elytron, and FIPS implementations the same priority `return 200;`, so a classpath exposing two full services silently selects whichever ServiceLoader enumerates first and runs the wrong backend; the strongest rebuttal is that deployment profiles normally isolate these providers, but the old code explicitly enforced that invariant and this new multi-provider design removes the enforcement.

authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:58 — P2 confidence 100 advisory: `implements CryptoProvider` couples a two-capability authorization-client adapter to the entire server crypto backend and makes every interface expansion and accidental call riskier; the strongest rebuttal is that the current client path needs only ECDSA conversion and keystores, but global service registration exposes the full type, while a narrow capability SPI or complete JCA delegate deletes all 17 unsupported branches and the places that must be updated for each future `CryptoProvider` method.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:30 — P1 confidence 75: the global first-writer guard `if (cryptoProvider == null)` permanently installs `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` when `AuthzClient` initializes through a loader that sees only its service, so later common-crypto calls deterministically reach one of its 17 `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.");` branches even after a full provider becomes visible.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that AuthzClient.create() calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()), and CryptoIntegration.init() has a first-writer-wins guard (if cryptoProvider == null). The AuthzClientCryptoProvider has order() returning 100, while other providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) return 200. If AuthzClient initializes first with a classloader that only sees AuthzClientCryptoProvider, that stub provider gets permanently installed. AuthzClientCryptoProvider has 17 methods throwing UnsupportedOperationException, so subsequent calls to those methods from other parts of the codebase would fail. This is a real initialization order bug where the limited stub provider can be permanently installed before a full provider becomes available.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that AuthzClientCryptoProvider implements the full CryptoProvider interface but only provides actual implementations for a few methods (getBouncyCastleProvider, order, getEcdsaCryptoProvider, getKeyStore), while 17+ other methods throw UnsupportedOperationException. This is a legitimate architectural concern - the class is registered via ServiceLoader as a CryptoProvider but most of its interface is non-functional. The diff shows this pattern clearly with numerous 'throw new UnsupportedOperationException' statements. However, this appears to be an intentional design choice for a minimal client-side crypto provider, and the order() method returning 100 (vs 200 for full providers) suggests it's meant to be lower priority. The concern about future CryptoProvider method additions requiring updates is valid but somewhat speculative.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:109 — P1 confidence 100: `System.arraycopy(signature, 0, r, 1, len);` throws unchecked ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException for a truncated attacker-supplied JOSE ECDSA signature, aborting verification instead of returning the declared IOException/failure result.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java lines 108-110, the code does `System.arraycopy(signature, 0, r, 1, len)` where `len = signLength / 2`. If an attacker provides a truncated signature where `signature.length < len`, this will throw an unchecked ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of the declared IOException. The method signature declares `throws IOException` but this runtime exception would bypass that, potentially causing unexpected behavior in signature verification. This is a real input validation bug in the new code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:133 — P2 confidence 100: `if (length == 0x80) { return -1; }` sends an indefinite-length INTEGER to `new byte[length]`, so malformed DER crashes with unchecked NegativeArraySizeException instead of the declared IOException.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at ASN1Decoder.java, the readLength() method at line 133 returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding (when length == 0x80). This value is then used in readInteger() which calls read(length) with length=-1. The read(int length) method at line 168 does `byte[] bytes = new byte[length]` which would throw NegativeArraySizeException (unchecked) instead of the declared IOException. This is a real bug where malformed DER input causes an unchecked exception rather than the expected IOException.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:73 — P2 confidence 100: `return new BigInteger(bytes);` throws unchecked NumberFormatException when a DER INTEGER declares length zero, so malformed signature input escapes the decoder's IOException contract and aborts its caller.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in ASN1Decoder.readInteger(), when readLength() returns 0 (which is valid per the code - length 0 is not explicitly rejected), the read(0) call returns an empty byte array, and `new BigInteger(bytes)` with an empty array throws NumberFormatException. This is an unchecked exception that would escape the IOException contract of the method. The diff shows this exact code path: readLength() can return 0 for a zero-length field, read(0) returns empty array, and BigInteger constructor throws on empty input.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:218 — Advisory P2 confidence 75: `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.");` makes AuthzClient work today only while shared crypto consumers use ECDSA conversion and fail immediately when a credential flow requests `getSignature`; although the provider is intentionally minimal, that rebuttal loses because it is installed as the process-wide `CryptoProvider` behind the full interface.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that AuthzClientCryptoProvider implements CryptoProvider interface but throws UnsupportedOperationException for most methods including getSignature(). The diff shows this provider is registered via META-INF/services and will be loaded by CryptoIntegration.init() when AuthzClient.create() is called. While the provider has order=100 (lower than other providers at 200), if no other provider is on the classpath, this minimal implementation becomes the process-wide CryptoProvider. The concern is valid - the provider only implements getEcdsaCryptoProvider() and getKeyStore() fully, but other code paths using CryptoIntegration.getProvider() would fail. However, this appears to be intentional design for a minimal client library, and the finding acknowledges this is 'intentionally minimal'. This is a legitimate architectural concern about the scope of the change rather than a bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:56 — P1 confidence 100: `Assert.assertArrayEquals(rsConcat, rsConcat2);` checks only that the new decoder and encoder reproduce their own intermediate representation, so paired semantic defects such as consistently reordered ECDSA components pass while the emitted DER signature fails verification; although round-trip equality checks byte preservation, only verifying `asn1Des` with the public key independently establishes protocol correctness.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test only verifies round-trip consistency (encode then decode produces the same intermediate bytes), but doesn't verify that the ASN1 DER output is actually valid and can be verified by standard signature verification. Looking at the test code in ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java lines 48-57, it signs data, converts to concatenated RS, then back to ASN1 DER, then back to concatenated RS, and only checks that rsConcat equals rsConcat2. This is a legitimate test coverage concern - the test doesn't verify that asn1Des can actually be used to verify the signature, which would catch semantic errors in the encoding. However, this is a test quality issue, not a bug in the production code itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:42 — P2 confidence 75 advisory: `keyPair = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair();` creates one provider-default curve for all three named tests, so `testES384` and `testES512` do not exercise their native 48-byte and 66-byte component boundaries and curve-specific conversion regressions ship undetected; although varying `algorithm.getSignatureLength()` exercises padding, it does not produce the actual scalar widths and sign-byte cases of P-384 and P-521.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test uses a single KeyPair generated with default EC parameters for all three test methods (ES256, ES384, ES512). Looking at the test code, `keyPair = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` in the constructor creates one key pair with default curve (likely P-256). While the tests do exercise different `algorithm.getSignatureLength()` values (64, 96, 132 bytes), they all use the same underlying key, so the actual signature bytes produced by the JCA Signature class will be for the default curve only. This means ES384 and ES512 tests don't truly test their respective P-384 and P-521 curves' scalar widths and edge cases. This is a legitimate test coverage concern for newly added crypto conversion logic, not a hallucination.
